title: Global Time Echoes: Distance-Structured Correlations in GNSS Clocks
abstract:
Phase-coherent spectral analysis of 62.7 million station-pair measurements from 364 GNSS stations (2023–2025; effective sample size N ≈ 25–28 independent distance bins after accounting for spatial correlation; see §Methods) reveals systematic distance-structured correlations in clock networks. These correlations follow an exponential decay with a Temporal Topology correlation length λ = 3,330–4,549 km (exponential best fit; bootstrap 95% CIs: CODE 1,198–5,918 km; IGS 3,197–4,871 km; ESA 2,532–3,984 km) and show strong goodness-of-fit when evaluated on distance-binned means across three distinct analysis center solutions on largely shared raw inputs (CODE, IGS Combined, ESA Final; R² = 0.920–0.970; fits are to bin means, not raw pairs). Cross-solution validation across software-diverse processing chains (Bernese, NAPEOS, and the IGS combination filter), consistent across 12 frequency bands and confirmed through multiple binning schemes and null hypothesis testing, demonstrates these patterns represent persistent empirical correlations not explained by the tested artifacts. The patterns also show dependencies on station elevation and geomagnetic latitude, consistent with screened scalar fields via continuous Temporal Topology: coherence strengthens and correlation lengths extend in quieter mid-latitude and higher-elevation regimes, while high ionospheric activity suppresses rather than generates the signal, and the forward-simulated satellite-visibility kernel is both broader and differently shaped (§4.6).

The primary inference rests on cross-centre distance-structured covariance and λ; the following planetary, Chandler, diurnal, and geomagnetic signatures provide complementary physical consistency tests. The correlations show associations with Earth's orbital motion (r = -0.571 to -0.793 across centers), planetary gravitational influences (8 nominally significant event fits, mostly non-event-locked on audit), Chandler wobble modulation (R² = 0.377–0.471), and systematic diurnal temporal variations with synchronized early morning coherence peaks (Local Solar Time). Comprehensive validation demonstrates 24–61× signal enhancement over randomized controls (z = 15.8–31.9 across 180 null test iterations), with 40.0–52.3% of 388 tests across 19 validation families surviving Bonferroni, empirical-Bayes, and false-discovery-rate corrections. TID exclusion analysis shows 21–23 % signal improvement when excluding high-ionosphere periods—confirming that ionospheric activity acts as a decohering screen on an underlying ground-clock correlation rather than its source (~78% ionosphere-independent baseline), consistent with shorter correlation lengths in the disturbed auroral band and local-night persistence bounding any residual static ionospheric contribution at ≲3% of the coherent signal.

The investigation was structured to test predictions from the Temporal Equivalence Principle (TEP) framework, which suggested a Temporal Topology correlation length (λ) of 1,000–10,000 km. The discriminating content is structural rather than the decade-wide prior interval itself: the pooled-band estimate λ = 3,330–4,549 km spans the geometric saturation radius R(M) ≈ 4,150 km, which is calibrated on this scale; the correlation is band-localized (control-band R² ≈ 0.6 vs ≈0.95 in the coherent bands), and the per-band decomposition is ordered (tidal-band λ ≈ 3,600–5,900 km declining through post-tidal ≈2,100–2,500 km to ≈1,050–1,450 km at intermediate frequencies, with the exponential fit degrading where coherence collapses). Forward simulation of the satellite-visibility and network-datum channel on the real station geometry bounds its effective decay scale at λ ≳ 6.7×10³ km; conditioned on the real product — true CODE ephemerides and the estimated satellite-clock content itself — the channel remains broader than every measured λ (no realisation below λ = 5,075 km across 40 conditioned realisations) and produces a profile shape (near-unity correlation within 1 Mm, sign-definite anticorrelation beyond ~5 Mm) that the measured correlation does not contain (§4.6). The measured terrestrial covariance scale defines the corpus's empirical saturation anchor ρ ≈ 20 g/cm³ (R(M) ≈ 4,150 km), which is then propagated without retuning across galactic and stellar regimes in Papers 6 and 11. Across products the fitted scale is conditioned by clock-product construction and estimator band floor: the multi-GNSS MGEX family returns λ = 1,862 ± 155 km, with controlled decomposition on identical station-days bounding spectral-resolution and common-mode contributions at ≲±25% while reproducing the same band-ordered profile and accounting for cross-product phase-index conditioning (Paper 14). The R comparison is therefore stated at the cross-product family level (~1.0–4.8×10³ km). Cross-pipeline consistency across software-diverse solutions, raw-RINEX pseudorange/SPP recovery (Paper 3), combined multi-GNSS product validation on a largely held-out 2025–2026 epoch (Paper 14), and the 25-year longitudinal recovery (Paper 2) establish the correlation structure across independent data reductions, observation epochs, and estimator architectures. Raw carrier-phase processing and non-GNSS optical-fiber and two-way satellite time-transfer (TWSTFT) links provide direct tests of the unsuppressed amplitude and baseline scaling across independent timing technologies. A companion 25-year longitudinal CODE analysis is presented at TEP-GNSS-II.

The empirically derived correlation length λ_T is a GNSS-sector covariance scale obtained after environmental projection and processing transfer. It is not the screening operator 𝒮_Σ(ℰ) itself, and it is not the non-exact (disformal) covariance term, which this measurement does not access.
